relations.note: Ea creates or perfects Adapa and grants extraordinary understanding, but not immortality.
Ea gives Adapa wisdom, effective speech, and knowledge of cosmic and ritual ordinances.
Adapa prepares provisions and the divine table and fishes for Ea’s household.
relations.date: Old Babylonian to seventh century BCE

relations.note: Ea teaches Adapa how to approach the gatekeepers and which heavenly offerings to refuse or accept.

relations.myth: Refusal of the food of life
relations.note: Ea calls the offerings deadly; whether this deceives or protects Adapa remains explicitly ambiguous.
Ilabrat calls Adapa Ea’s son, probably expressing patronage or functional sonship rather than biological descent.

relations.myth: Judgment for breaking the South Wind’s wing
relations.note: Anu summons and interrogates Adapa after learning that his curse stopped the South Wind.

relations.myth: Offer of the food of life
relations.note: Anu offers Adapa life-giving food and water, clothing, and oil; Adapa accepts only clothing and oil.
Damaged endings variously suggest Anu returned Adapa to earth or favorably installed him in heaven.

relations.myth: Report of the broken South Wind
relations.note: Ilabrat identifies Adapa to Anu as Ea’s son and the breaker of the South Wind’s wing.
Adapa claims to mourn Dumuzi’s disappearance; pleased or astonished, Dumuzi supports him before Anu.
Adapa claims to mourn Ningishzida’s disappearance; the gatekeeper commends his speech and helps calm Anu.

relations.myth: Healing after the South Wind’s restoration
relations.note: Ninkarrak heals disease associated with the restored South Wind, though no direct dialogue with Adapa survives.
A ritual speaker identifies as Adapa alongside a damaged claim of representing Asalluhi.

relations.myth: Divine assembly over the South Wind
relations.note: Adapa appears amid the great gods’ assembly, but no individually recoverable exchange with the collective survives.
The South Wind overturns Adapa’s boat; his effective curse breaks its wing and stops it for seven days.
Late learned texts combine Uanna with Adapa, though Adapa may function there as an epithet meaning wise.
Adapa was later fused with Berossus’s amphibious culture-bringer through the learned Uanna-Adapa equation.
Adapa’s heavenly journey resembles Utuabzu’s ascent, prompting later conflation despite no secure identity.
First-millennium traditions assimilate Adapa to the primeval sages as member, epithet, or counterpart.
